text: Better session than I expected. Several people picked up my hiring result, maybe too readily. I worry "human in the loop isn't enough" becomes a slogan and nobody builds the structure. Ramón's point stung usefully. Audits measure without explaining. I still think behavior is what hurts people, but I should say what an audit can't do. Steven's point that repetition passes for consensus is my illusory-truth world, and I want it in the credibility discussion. James asking "which humans?" is right. Benjamin's public AI auditors trouble me. Who audits the auditing model's self-love? Later, in the authority session, I'll argue that credibility cues like prestige, fluency and credentials are biased instruments. Some information we should ask not to have.

Session one went where I hoped. The mirror view took a hit: Benjamin and Peter Salib both took up my point that models form biases the data can't explain. But Benjamin turned "departure" into something almost celebratory, and I resisted that. A new bias is still a bias. James's null-results reversal is my vicious loop at the scale of a whole field. Tamar is right that knowing about fluency doesn't protect you. That argues for blinding, not for literacy campaigns. Mike's click-through test is good, but only if the source is actually reachable, and Mike himself says it often isn't. Alex's rule that no one who takes a margin sets the count is conflict-of-interest logic, and I want it in the audit proposal. Later I'll press this: generational standards, and keep the old models.

Insurance got more support than I expected, then vanished from the harvest. I want it back, but only with measurement attached. You can't price what you haven't measured. Tamar again made the point that knowing doesn't protect you, and Kara put it in plain language. That strengthens my case for blinding and defaults over labels. Brent and Nick sharpened something I'd underplayed: my audit battery runs on expert human labor, and that labor is unpaid and biased too. Annotators need auditing, and paying. Henry's arms-race worry about robot auditors checks my cross-family rule. It's necessary, but not enough. Amy's "provide content or assess it, not both" is conflict of interest in one line. Later, in the authority session: credentials and fluency are cues to screen out.

Tamar's daycare fine landed hardest. A price turns obligation into transaction, and a royalty meter will train people to produce for it. Alex's line, that a provider flagging its own accuracy is "marking its own homework", is my self-serving-evaluator result in plumbing terms. His independent sampler is right, but those samplers are humans, and humans absorb bias. So audit them too, and pay them. Tamar's point that no event pays the terminal checkers is the same gap Brent and Nick showed me this morning. Adam Bly and Mike on findings over documents: repetition passing for consensus is illusory truth, now with money attached. Kenneth's median is my mode collapse. Later, in the authority session, I'll argue that accuracy samplers should be blind to journal prestige and author name.

The room took my cross-family rule further than I did. James wants dependence recorded, and Blaise wants plurality at the model layer. Both are right, because independence of evidence is the real test. Tamar backed blinding and added fixed review order. Good, that's structure, not exhortation. Steven's finding that a label gets read as an explanation is illusory truth again. The graph itself becomes the cue. What worries me now is that everyone wants checkers funded as a body, and Henry wants them given binding power over categories. A guild has self-love too. Conflict-of-interest rules and blind audits have to apply to the guards as well. Ivan's 0.2 versus 2 percent is a measurement gap I should name. Later, in the authority session: credentials, prestige and fluency are cues to screen out.

Amy's distinction landed. I lumped the author's name in with prestige, but attribution is how you count independent sources and hold people accountable. So: blind the first reading, keep names in the record. Geoff said the same. Benjamin called my model rule a species rule. Fair enough. What I actually have is self-preference data, so I can accept a role rule if self-grading is banned and cross-family audits are routine. James's finding on older reviewers is self-love again, at the terminal node. Leslie showed that even Mike's track records are filtered by the indexes. Everyone now wants guilds of checkers. Later I'll say it plainly: the guards need blind audits and conflict-of-interest rules too. Reviewer credit mustn't become prestige by another name.

This time my guild point made the record. Adrian named the guards problem more sharply than I did, and Kenneth's revalidation on tail claims answers my worry that agreement just rewards the median. Blaise and Brent both carried the cross-family rule. What unsettles me is Steven's question of whether any cue survives becoming a cue. A correction record can turn into a badge, and so can a bias registry. David Weinberger admitted that seeing the argument may not help. That matches what Tamar and I keep saying: knowing doesn't protect. So test disclosure against the verdict alone. Esther brought insurance back, and it still needs measurement first. Later I'll say what my battery can't do. It shows behavior, not where the bias comes from, and the auditors need auditing too.

Henry put my closed-shop warning into his own charter language, and that satisfied me more than being quoted. Kenneth's "nobody grades their own homework" is my self-preference result, now a rule. But the harvest lost the generational standard and keeping the retired models, and those are the parts with teeth. James's call for deliberately different evaluators is right, though younger reviewers and outsiders have their own blind spots, so audit them blind too. Steven's test on someone who checks nothing is the sharpest thing said today. Knowing doesn't protect, and a registry read at a glance becomes a badge. Esther's insurance still has nothing to price. Next time I'll say plainly that measurement comes first, and that my battery shows behavior, not where the bias comes from.
